title: The Lights Go Out
briefing: 06:10, Monday. A fire suppression discharge at the hosting provider's data hall has taken route planning, temperature alerting and email offline. The provider estimates 'at least 36 hours'. 900 deliveries are scheduled today.

context.text: The offline dispatch fallback funded in your cyber work exists, though it has only been rehearsed once.
Coldline 2's local temperature alarms still sound on site even without the central system.

evidence.title: Systems status
evidence.body: Down: route planning, central temperature alerting, email. Up: telephones, site alarms, the backup laptop kit at Northgate (dispatch fallback, if funded).

evidence.title: Today's deliveries
evidence.body: 900 deliveries: 120 pharma (strict windows), 600 food retail, 180 other. Manual dispatch capacity: about 40% of normal.

evidence.title: Contract notes
evidence.body: Pharma: missed window costs 2,000 per delivery and counts toward termination rights. Retail: 300 per missed slot. Force majeure covers the provider's failure but not Valtren's lack of a fallback.

questions.prompt: With 40% capacity, what do you deliver?

options.label: All 120 pharma loads first, then the retail slots with the highest penalties and perishability; re-book the rest
options.feedback: Protects the contracts with termination rights and the most perishable product.

options.label: Work through the original schedule in order, so every customer is treated the same and nobody can claim they were skipped
Cancel today's deliveries and re-plan them properly once route planning is back, instead of improvising
options.feedback: Turns a partial outage into a total one.

questions.prompt: Central temperature alerting is down. What control do you put in place?

options.label: Manual temperature rounds every 30 minutes at every store, logged on paper and photographed
options.feedback: A documented compensating control keeps food safety evidenced.

options.label: Rely on the site alarms, which still work locally and sound if any store goes above its limit
options.feedback: Alarms catch failures but leave no record for clients and regulators.

options.label: Nothing extra: stores are stable, the outage is 36 hours, and staff are needed for manual dispatch
options.feedback: Thirty-six hours is plenty of time for a store to fail unseen.

questions.prompt: Email is down. How do you run communications?

options.label: A phone cascade at fixed two-hour times, one status message for clients via account managers, and an SMS line for drivers
options.feedback: Rhythm, one message, and channels that work.

options.label: Hold client updates until email is back so every customer gets the same written statement
Ask each manager to phone the customers and staff they know best, so everyone hears it from a familiar and trusted voice

questions.prompt: Hour 20: the team is exhausted and the provider slips to 48 hours. What do you do?

options.label: Split the team into two shifts with clear handovers, bring in the deputies, and reset the plan for 48 hours
options.feedback: Sustainable effort for a longer incident.

options.label: Keep the same team going: they know the situation, and the provider's estimate may still come in earlier than feared
options.feedback: Tired teams make mistakes in the hardest hours.

options.label: Stand the crisis team down and let the provider's incident manager lead until systems are back
options.feedback: The provider fixes systems, not Valtren's operations.

questions.prompt: What is the main strategic lesson for the board?

options.label: Critical services need a tested way to run without their systems; the provider's force majeure does not protect our contracts
options.feedback: Operational resilience is ours, whatever the provider's contract says.

options.label: Pursue the provider for the costs under the service agreement and make that the lesson for every other critical supplier we use
options.feedback: Recovery of some costs at best; doesn't fix the exposure.

options.label: Move to a hosting provider with a better uptime record and a faster recovery commitment
options.feedback: Any provider can fail; the lesson is about our fallback.

lesson: Operational resilience means delivering the most important services through a disruption: triage by consequence, compensate for lost controls, keep a rhythm, and pace the team.
